claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
The proposed framework combines microstructural descriptors, machine learning, limited high-fidelity calculations or experiments, and micromechanical finite-element modeling.
Local descriptors of chemical and structural fluctuations can be extracted from high-resolution imaging or simulation.
A machine-learning model trained on a small high-fidelity dataset can rapidly predict local mechanical properties.
Spatially varying properties predicted by machine learning can be incorporated into a finite-element model to simulate macroscopic tensile and fracture responses.
Multilevel chemical fluctuations in the hierarchical heterostructure produce locally variable stiffness and defect sensitivity.
Local chemical and structural variations govern local elastic stiffness.
Local chemical and structural variations govern the initiation sites of plasticity and fracture.

Embedding spatially varying, machine-learning-predicted properties in a finite-element model will improve predictions of overall elastic and inelastic response, including crack initiation and propagation.
The data-informed surrogate approach will reduce reliance on extensive full-scale calculations.

Relative to full first-principles/CALPHAD methods or isolated machine-learning models, the hybrid framework will lower prediction RMSE for Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness by at least approximately 20%.
The hybrid framework will reduce computational time by nearly an order of magnitude relative to traditional full-scale methods.
The hybrid framework will capture fracture-related behavior that existing models often miss.
Existing first-principles, CALPHAD, or isolated machine-learning approaches commonly represent idealized defect-free crystals or omit hierarchical-heterostructure effects.
The framework is expected to remain reliable when its descriptors capture the mechanically relevant heterogeneities and test temperature and strain rate remain within the training regime.
Model accuracy may degrade after heterostructural changes caused by thermal aging or extreme environments.
Model accuracy may degrade at temperatures or loading rates far outside the training domain.
The resolution and quality of the input microstructural data affect model performance.
